0.title: The Art and Science of Biblical Interpretation
0.overview:
Hermeneutics — from the Greek hermeneuo, to interpret or explain — is the discipline of reading the Bible well. Every time you open Scripture and ask "What does this mean?" you are doing hermeneutics, whether or not you know it. The question is not whether you will interpret the Bible but whether you will do it carefully, consistently, and faithfully.

The stakes are high. The history of the church is in large part a history of interpretive decisions — about the relationship of the Testaments, about prophecy and fulfillment, about the genre of apocalyptic literature, about the application of Old Testament law. Virtually every major theological dispute in church history has an underlying hermeneutical dimension. People are not usually arguing about the text — they have read it. They are arguing about what it means and how it works.

This study is organised around six core skills and questions: (1) the foundations — why interpretation is necessary and what guides it; (2) the grammatical-historical method — the bedrock approach shared by virtually all evangelical interpreters; (3) biblical theology — reading each text within the whole-Bible story; (4) typology and prophecy — how the Old Testament anticipates and the New Testament fulfills; (5) Reformed and Dispensational hermeneutics — how two major evangelical traditions interpret the same text differently; (6) preaching and application — moving faithfully from the ancient text to the contemporary congregation.

The goal is not merely academic competence but pastoral faithfulness: the preacher and teacher who handles the Word of God well is handling a living sword, and the congregation that hears it well-handled is being formed by the only voice that can truly change a human heart.

1.title: Foundations: Why We Need Hermeneutics
1.overview:
Some Christians resist the idea that Bible interpretation requires a discipline and a method. "Just read it plainly," they say — as though the Bible is self-interpreting and the reader is a neutral receiver of its obvious meaning. This instinct is admirable in its reverence for Scripture, but it is mistaken in its understanding of how language, history, and human cognition actually work.

The Bible is an ancient document — composed across fifteen centuries, in three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek), by some forty authors, in cultures radically different from our own. Its genres include narrative, law, poetry, wisdom literature, prophecy, apocalyptic, epistle, and gospel. Every one of these genres follows its own conventions, and the reader who does not know those conventions will misread the text as surely as someone who reads a classified advertisement expecting the conventions of poetry.

The Holy Spirit is the supreme interpreter of Scripture — Christ promised to lead his disciples into all truth (John 16:13), and the Spirit illumines the minds of believers to understand and receive what is written. But the Spirit's illumination does not bypass human faculties; it works through them. The Spirit who inspired the original authors to write in Hebrew and Greek expects readers to take those languages seriously. Careful interpretation is not a lack of trust in the Spirit — it is the form that trust takes.

Three preliminary convictions shape everything: (1) The Bible means what its original human authors intended — meaning is not infinitely fluid or wholly reader-determined. (2) The divine author's meaning may transcend the human author's full awareness — the Spirit can deposit in a text more than the human author consciously intended, especially in prophecy. (3) Scripture interprets Scripture — the clearer passages are the lens through which we read the less clear.
1.theology:
The analogy of faith: The Reformers articulated the principle of analogia fidei — Scripture interprets Scripture. No passage should be interpreted in isolation from the whole. A difficult or obscure text should be read in light of clearer texts on the same subject. This prevents both eccentric interpretation (building a theology on a single difficult text) and atomistic interpretation (treating each passage as independent of all others).

The perspicuity of Scripture: The Westminster Confession (I.7) affirms that "those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed for salvation are so clearly propounded and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of the ordinary means, may attain unto a sufficient understanding of them." Scripture's essential message is clear enough for the ordinary reader; its depths reward the most diligent scholar. Both are true, and neither cancels the other.

The role of the Spirit: 1 Corinthians 2:14 states that the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God — they are spiritually discerned. Illumination is not merely intellectual; it is the Spirit opening the heart to receive what the mind has understood. The regenerate reader has an advantage the unregenerate scholar lacks: not superior intelligence but the indwelling Spirit who bears witness to the truth of what is read.
1.examples:
The Ethiopian eunuch: Acts 8:30–31 — Philip finds the eunuch reading Isaiah 53 and asks: "Do you understand what you are reading?" The eunuch's honest reply: "How can I, unless someone guides me?" This is the human condition before God's Word. The text is clear enough to raise the question (the eunuch knows he is reading about someone's suffering); it is not clear enough — without context, without the whole story, without a guide — to identify the referent. Philip's guidance — drawing the whole-Bible story together — is the act of a biblical theologian and a skilled interpreter. Every preacher is called to be Philip.

Peter on Paul: 2 Peter 3:15–16 — Peter acknowledges that Paul's letters contain "some things hard to understand" that the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction. Even the apostle who walked with Jesus acknowledged that Scripture is sometimes difficult. Difficulty is not an embarrassment — it is an invitation to more careful work. The interpreter who thinks all difficulties are easily resolved has not yet read carefully enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The image is striking: rightly handling (orthotomounta — literally, cutting straight) the word of truth, as a craftsman cuts a straight line, or as a road-builder cuts the most direct path through difficult terrain. The alternative — cutting crookedly — is not merely a technical failure; it is a shame before God. This means that sloppy interpretation is not merely an intellectual failing but a moral one. The pastor who preaches the text carelessly, who does not do the work of finding out what it means before telling others what it means, is handling carelessly the Word that God breathed out. The word worker is deliberate: good interpretation is labour.

verseByVerse.quote: They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the earliest descriptions of biblical interpretation in Scripture itself. The Levites read clearly — the text was made audible and intelligible. They gave the sense — they explained what the text meant. The people understood the reading — the goal was achieved: understanding in the congregation. This three-stage process (text → sense → understanding) maps perfectly onto the preacher's task: read the text accurately, explain what it means, and make it comprehensible to those who hear. The text that is read but not given sense leaves the congregation where the Ethiopian eunuch was — aware that something important is being said, but unable to say what.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit is the ultimate interpreter. He inspired the Word; he illumines the reader; he applies the text to the conscience. This does not make careful interpretation unnecessary — the Spirit who inspired Paul's careful argumentation in Romans is not honoured by careless reading of it. But it does mean that interpretation is never merely a human intellectual exercise. The interpreter who does not pray before opening the text is working without their most important resource. And the congregation that hears the text preached is being addressed not only by a human voice but by the Spirit who gave the text and now makes it live.

verseByVerse.quote: The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The most sophisticated unbelieving scholar can parse the Greek of John's Gospel with technical precision and still not receive its truth. Illumination is not the same as intellectual comprehension — it is the Spirit's work of opening the heart to embrace what the mind has grasped. This has a crucial pastoral implication: the congregation that has not yet received the Spirit cannot be argued into understanding by more clever exposition. They need the Spirit. The preacher who knows this prays for the Spirit's work even as they prepare the sermon, and trusts that the same Spirit who inspired the text is present in the congregation to make it land.

2.title: The Grammatical-Historical Method
2.overview:
The grammatical-historical method is the bedrock of evangelical biblical interpretation, shared — in its essential commitments — by Reformed, Baptist, Lutheran, Anglican, Dispensational, and most other evangelical traditions. It rests on two convictions: that the meaning of a text is found in its words (grammar), and that those words were written in a specific historical situation that shapes their meaning (history).

The grammatical dimension attends to the words themselves: their precise meaning in the original language, the significance of verb tenses and moods, the force of prepositions, the structure of the argument. Greek and Hebrew are not merely useful extras for the serious student of Scripture — they are the languages in which God chose to speak, and every translation, however excellent, is already an interpretation. The preacher who has not learned to use Greek and Hebrew tools — lexicons, commentaries, grammars — is working with a translation of a translation.

The historical dimension asks: who wrote this? To whom? In what circumstances? What questions were they addressing? What would the original readers have heard? Every text has an original context — an implied author, an implied audience, an occasion, a purpose — and the interpreter who ignores this context is a traveller without a map. The letters of Paul were written to specific churches facing specific crises; the prophecies of Isaiah were addressed to specific kings in specific geopolitical situations. Their meaning does not evaporate into timelessness — it is historically rooted and must be understood historically before it can be applied universally.

Crucially, the grammatical-historical method does not mean that a text has only one application — it means that a text has one meaning (the author's intended meaning) from which many applications may flow. The preacher's task is to find the one meaning and then draw out the many applications for the specific congregation in the specific moment.
2.theology:
Authorial intent: The grammatical-historical method is committed to authorial intent as the ground of meaning. This puts it in direct opposition to reader-response theories (meaning is what the reader makes of the text) and to allegorical interpretation (meaning is a spiritual sense hidden behind the literal). E.D. Hirsch's influential argument in Validity in Interpretation (1967) — that meaning belongs to the author, significance to the reader — maps closely onto the evangelical hermeneutical commitment: the text means what its author intended; its significance for us is derived from, not imposed upon, that meaning.

Genre recognition: Part of the historical task is identifying the genre of the passage being interpreted. Narrative works differently from epistle; poetry works differently from law; apocalyptic works differently from wisdom literature. Reading apocalyptic prophecy with the genre conventions of newspaper reporting produces bizarre results — and has produced, historically, enormous damage (date-setting, political allegory). Reading the Psalms as propositional doctrinal statements misses their character as inspired prayers and meditations. Genre is not merely a literary nicety — it is a key to the text's meaning.

The original audience: Before we ask "What does this mean for me?" we must ask "What did this mean for them?" The congregation at Philippi heard Paul's letter to them with specific ears — they knew Paul, they knew their own situation, they knew the Roman imperial context that shaped phrases like "our citizenship is in heaven" (Phil 3:20). Recovering that original hearing is the historical task. The application for us flows from what it meant for them.
2.examples:
Acts 2 and the gift of tongues: Was the miracle at Pentecost a miracle of speaking (the disciples spoke in languages they had not learned) or a miracle of hearing (the crowd heard their own language)? The grammar of Acts 2 is clear: the disciples spoke in other tongues (v.4), and the crowd each heard in their own language (v.6). Both happened. The grammatical-historical method works through the precise language before building a theology of glossolalia. Interpretive disputes about spiritual gifts often begin with insufficient attention to the precise text.

"Do not muzzle the ox" (1 Cor 9:9): Paul quotes Deuteronomy 25:4 and asks: "Is it for oxen that God is concerned?" Using the grammatical-historical method, we note that Paul is not denying concern for oxen — he is doing what the original text intended: establishing a principle (workers deserve their wages) that applies across domains. The Deuteronomy law is not merely about agricultural practice; it encodes a moral principle that the New Testament applies to gospel workers. This is a controlled application, derived from the text's own original logic.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is one of the most important test cases for evangelical hermeneutics. Grammatically, the Hebrew word almah means young woman of marriageable age (implicitly a virgin in its cultural context); Matthew 1:23 quotes the Septuagint's parthenos (virgin) and applies it to Mary. Historically, the prophecy was addressed to Ahaz in the context of the Syro-Ephraimite crisis (735 BC) and appears to have had some near-term fulfillment. The question is how these two dimensions — near-term sign and ultimate fulfillment in Christ — relate. This is the contested terrain of typological and prophetic interpretation, explored in Unit 4.

verseByVerse.quote: For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A straightforward grammatical-historical observation changes the reading of this familiar verse. The phrase fall short is present tense in the Greek — not past (have fallen short, implying a once-for-all event) but ongoing (keep falling short, as a present reality). Universal sinfulness is not merely a historical fact about humanity's past; it is the present condition. And the glory of God — what we fall short of — is the image-bearing glory we were created to reflect. Sin is the failure to be fully human; it is the loss of the likeness of God that we were made to display. This reading enriches what might otherwise seem a simple statement of depravity.

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The grammar here matters enormously for the doctrine of faith. The demonstrative pronoun this (touto) is neuter in Greek. Both grace (charis) and faith (pistis) are feminine. This means this cannot refer grammatically to faith alone or grace alone — it refers to the whole complex: this salvation-by-grace-through-faith is the gift of God. Some have used this verse to argue that faith itself is the specific gift; the grammar will not quite bear that, though other texts (Phil 1:29) do support it. The grammatical-historical method is precise: we do not build doctrine on grammatical observations that the grammar does not support, but we do allow grammar to clarify what is actually being claimed.

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the Bible's first verse rewards grammatical-historical attention. The Hebrew bereshit (in the beginning) may be understood as an absolute statement (at the absolute beginning) or as a temporal clause (when God began to create). The genre of Genesis 1 — whether it is historical narrative, theological framework, or something else — is itself a hermeneutical question that significantly affects how one reads the days of creation. The grammatical-historical interpreter does not bypass these questions with a simple appeal to literalism — they engage them, because the text itself demands engagement. Faithful interpretation begins with honest reading.

3.title: Biblical Theology: Reading the Whole Story
3.overview:
Biblical theology is not merely theology that is "biblical" (in the sense of being faithful to Scripture — systematic theology aspires to that too). It is a specific discipline: the study of how the Bible's message develops across the canon, from Genesis to Revelation, as a unified story of God's redemptive purposes. Where systematic theology asks "What does the whole Bible teach about X?" biblical theology asks "How does the Bible's teaching about X develop and unfold through the progressive stages of redemptive history?"

The foundational conviction of biblical theology is that the Bible is not merely a collection of disconnected books but a unified narrative — one story, told by one divine Author through many human authors, moving toward one climax: the person and work of Jesus Christ. This means that no passage of Scripture can be fully understood in isolation from its place in the larger story. Levitical sacrifice makes full sense only when you see it as pointing forward to the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ. The Davidic kingship makes full sense only when you see it as the anticipation of the eternal King. The Exodus makes full sense only when you see it as the pattern that the greater Exodus (Luke 9:31) fulfills.

The great biblical theologians — Geerhardus Vos, Edmund Clowney, Graeme Goldsworthy, D.A. Carson, and Tom Schreiner — have shown that the Bible's story has a shape: creation, fall, redemption, new creation. Every book, every passage, every character exists within this arc. The interpreter who knows the arc reads every text with their peripheral vision engaged: where does this fit in the story? What came before that it depends on? What comes after that it anticipates?
3.theology:
Promise and fulfillment: The engine of biblical theology is the dynamic of promise and fulfillment. God makes promises — to Adam and Eve (Gen 3:15), to Abraham (Gen 12:1–3), to David (2 Sam 7:12–16) — and the rest of the Bible traces the history of those promises moving toward their ultimate fulfillment in Christ. This means that the Old Testament is not merely background for the New — it is the promise of which the New Testament is the fulfillment, and the New Testament cannot be fully understood apart from it.

Typology: A type is a divinely intended pattern — a person, event, or institution in the Old Testament that prefigures its antitype in the New. Adam is a type of Christ (Rom 5:14); the Passover lamb is a type of Christ (1 Cor 5:7); the tabernacle is a type of Christ's incarnate body (John 2:21) and of the heavenly sanctuary (Heb 9:24). Typology is not allegory — it is not reading foreign meanings into the text; it is recognising the pattern that God himself wove into history and that the New Testament authors explicitly identify.

The covenants as the structure of the story: Reformed biblical theology typically reads the Bible's story through the lens of the covenants: the Covenant of Works (Adam), the Covenant of Grace (post-Fall, administered through Noah, Abraham, Moses, and David, and fulfilled in Christ), and the New Covenant (inaugurated at the Last Supper, sealed in Christ's blood, awaiting its full consummation). The covenants are not merely legal arrangements but relational bonds — the form in which God has structured his relationship with humanity across redemptive history.
3.examples:
Goldsworthy's Gospel quadrilateral: Graeme Goldsworthy defines the gospel as "God's people in God's place under God's rule." This simple pattern — people, place, rule — first appears in Eden, is partially restored in Israel (God's people, in the land of Canaan, under God's law), is fulfilled in Christ (the true Israel, in the new creation, under the reign of God), and will be consummated in the new Jerusalem (Rev 21:3). Every major passage of the Old Testament can be plotted on this grid and seen as a movement toward or a partial expression of the gospel pattern.

Clowney on Christ in all the Scriptures: Edmund Clowney's The Unfolding Mystery traces the promise of Christ through the Old Testament — in the seed of the woman (Gen 3:15), the blessing of Abraham (Gen 12:1–3), the Prophet like Moses (Deut 18:15), the Son of David (2 Sam 7), the Suffering Servant (Isa 53), the Son of Man (Dan 7). Each text adds a facet to the portrait of the coming One. The interpreter who knows this progression reads the New Testament not as a surprise but as the answer to a question that the whole Old Testament has been asking.

verseByVerse.quote: And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The risen Christ is the first biblical theologian — or rather, he reveals that biblical theology was his Father's design all along. Beginning with Moses (the Pentateuch) and moving through all the Prophets, he showed how all the Scriptures speak of him. Not some of them. Not the obviously messianic passages. All of them. This is the charter of Christ-centred biblical theology: every part of the Old Testament has something to say about him — directly, typologically, by contrast, by promise, by pattern. The interpreter who reads the Old Testament without asking "where is Christ in this?" has not yet learned to read with Jesus as their teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Mosaic law had a historical function — guardian (paidagogos — a tutor or escort who supervised a child until maturity) — that was temporary by design. It was not the final form of God's relationship with his people; it was the penultimate form, pointing toward and preparing for Christ. This is a foundational biblical-theological claim: the Old Testament is structured for Christ, not merely prior to him. The law's sacrificial system tutored Israel in the meaning of atonement; its holiness code defined the shape of the life God required; its failure (Israel's persistent disobedience) prepared the soil for the one who would perfectly obey and perfectly atone.

verseByVerse.quote: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The opening of Hebrews is a biblical-theological statement in miniature. God spoke — at many times, in many ways, progressively, partially — through the prophets. Now he has spoken finally, fully, climactically, in a Son. The Son is not one more instalment in an ongoing series; he is the telos, the one toward whom all the prior speech was moving. The Hebrews interpreter must read the whole Old Testament as the preparation for this speech, and must read every subsequent text as the unpacking of what has been spoken in the Son. Biblical theology gives you the map; the Son is the destination.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The end of the story echoes its beginning. God and humanity in unmediated fellowship — the Garden of Eden, the Tabernacle, the Temple, the Incarnation — all anticipate this final reality: the dwelling place of God with man, permanently, without veil, without exile, without sin. The whole biblical story is the story of God coming to dwell with his people — driven out, drawing near, incarnate, indwelling by the Spirit, and finally, in the new creation, present with a fullness that no prior dwelling anticipated. The interpreter who knows this story reads every passage of Scripture in light of where it is all headed.

4.title: Typology and Prophecy: Old Testament Anticipation
4.overview:
One of the most fascinating and sometimes contested areas of biblical interpretation is the relationship between Old Testament texts and their New Testament fulfillment. Matthew's Gospel repeatedly uses the formula "that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet" — attaching Old Testament texts to events in Jesus' life in ways that sometimes puzzle modern readers. Was the prophet actually predicting this event? Or is Matthew doing something else?

Understanding the answer requires two tools: typology and a nuanced understanding of Old Testament prophecy. Typology, as we saw in Unit 3, is the reading of divinely intended patterns — real historical people, events, and institutions that foreshadow their New Testament antitype. Prophecy is direct verbal prediction — God speaking through his prophets about what will happen. Sometimes these overlap; often they operate distinctly.

Old Testament prophecy frequently has a multi-layered fulfillment structure. A prophecy may have a near-term, partial fulfillment within the Old Testament period and an ultimate, final fulfillment in Christ. This is sometimes called the near-far structure of prophecy, or sensus plenior (fuller sense) — the divine author intends a depth of meaning that goes beyond (but does not contradict) the human author's awareness. Isaiah 7:14 is the classic example: Ahaz received a sign in his own time, but the ultimate Immanuel — God truly with us — is only fulfilled in the Incarnation.

The New Testament authors were not reading the Old Testament carelessly or creatively — they were reading it as Jesus taught them to: as a text that, at every level, speaks of him. Their interpretive moves follow patterns that, once learned, become the interpreter's own tools. Christological interpretation of the Old Testament is not eisegesis (reading in) but the deepest form of exegesis (reading out) — discovering what the divine Author encoded in the text.
4.theology:
Sensus plenior: The "fuller sense" refers to the additional depth of meaning that the divine Author intended in a text beyond the human author's conscious awareness. This is not a license for arbitrary spiritualising — the fuller sense must be consistent with the literal sense, must be drawn out by the canonical context (especially the New Testament), and must follow the pattern of the text's own logic. The human author of Psalm 22 was expressing genuine personal anguish; the divine Author was anticipating the cry of the Son of God from the cross. Both meanings are real; neither cancels the other.

Correspondence and escalation: When the New Testament fulfills an Old Testament type or prophecy, the fulfillment is always greater than the anticipation — it corresponds in form but escalates in reality. The Passover lamb was real and significant; the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world is infinitely greater. The manna in the wilderness sustained life for forty years; the Bread of Life gives eternal life. The Temple housed the divine presence behind a veil; Christ is Immanuel — God with us — unveiled.

Israel and the nations: A significant hermeneutical question concerns how the Old Testament promises to Israel are fulfilled. Do promises about the land, the city, the Temple, and the restored nation refer to the literal geography of the Middle East and a literal national Israel? Or are they typologically fulfilled in Christ and his worldwide, multiethnic church? This is the central point at which Reformed and Dispensational hermeneutics diverge — explored fully in Unit 5.
4.examples:
Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15: "Out of Egypt I called my son" (Hosea 11:1) originally refers to the Exodus — God calling Israel out of Egypt. Matthew applies it to Jesus' return from Egypt (Matt 2:15) with his formula "that it might be fulfilled." Was Hosea predicting Jesus' childhood? Contextually, Hosea was narrating Israel's history. Matthew is doing something more subtle: Jesus is the true Israel, reliving Israel's story and succeeding where Israel failed. The Exodus pattern is not merely historical — it is the pattern into which the Son of God enters and brings to its ultimate expression. Matthew's use is typological fulfillment, not prediction-fulfillment.

Isaiah 53 and the Servant: Here the hermeneutical waters run deep. The Servant in Isaiah 40–55 is sometimes Israel (Isa 41:8), sometimes an individual within Israel who suffers on behalf of the nation (Isa 52:13–53:12). The New Testament identifies this suffering Servant explicitly with Jesus (Acts 8:32–35). The grammatical-historical reading of Isaiah 53 — attending to the specific details of vicarious suffering, substitutionary death, and vindication — yields the portrait of one who bears others' iniquities. The New Testament does not import a foreign meaning; it reveals the divine intention encoded in the text from the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The word fulfill (pleroō) is doing enormous work here. Jesus did not come to cancel the Old Testament — he came to bring it to its intended fullness and completion. This has implications for how the Old Testament law functions for the Christian: not abolished (its moral content remains binding in principle) but fulfilled (its ceremonial and civil dimensions find their completion in Christ and his new covenant community). The interpreter who understands this text does not treat the Old Testament as irrelevant (abolish) or treat it as though Christ had not come (ignore fulfillment). They read it as what it is: the forward-leaning Word that has now arrived at its destination.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things happened to them as examples, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul explicitly authorises typological interpretation — the events of the Exodus and wilderness wandering (these things) happened as types (tupoi — patterns, examples) and were written for the instruction of New Testament believers. This is remarkable: Paul is saying that the purpose of those historical events included their literary function — God not only acted in history but ensured that those acts were written down as patterns for future generations. The interpreter who reads the Old Testament looking for these patterns is not imposing a foreign method — they are following the apostle's own interpretive practice.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The tabernacle and temple were not merely religious institutions — they were copies (antitupa — antitypes, models) of heavenly realities. The earthly sanctuary was real and significant; the heavenly sanctuary that it modeled is infinitely greater. This typological relationship was not visible to the original builders of the tabernacle — it is revealed by the Spirit through the author of Hebrews. The principle applies broadly: the Old Testament institutions are not ends in themselves but shadows cast backward by the coming glory of Christ. The interpreter who reads Exodus and Leviticus with this in view will find there a depth of christological meaning that repays a lifetime of attention.

verseByVerse.quote: But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Centuries before the cross, the Spirit of God described it with a precision that staggers the believing reader. Pierced — for our transgressions. Crushed — for our iniquities. Chastisement — for our peace. Wounds — for our healing. The prepositions are substitutionary: all that we deserved fell on him; all that he deserved — peace, healing — came to us. This text does not merely predict the cross; it interprets it — telling us what the cross means before it happens, so that when it happens we will not miss the meaning. The Ethiopian eunuch who read this and asked "about whom does the prophet say this?" was doing precisely the right thing. Philip answered: this is Jesus.

5.title: Reformed and Dispensational Hermeneutics: A Respectful Comparison
5.overview:
Two of the most significant and widespread evangelical hermeneutical traditions are Reformed (covenant-theological) interpretation and Dispensational interpretation. Both traditions are committed to the authority and inerrancy of Scripture, both use the grammatical-historical method as their foundational approach, and both have produced scholars, pastors, and preachers of the highest order. Their differences are real and significant — but they are the differences of people reading the same Bible with genuine seriousness, not the differences between faith and faithlessness.

Understanding both traditions — their underlying commitments, their characteristic moves, and the texts they each handle most naturally — is essential for the pastor who serves a congregation shaped by both. Many believers hold their hermeneutical commitments instinctively, absorbed from the teachers and traditions that formed them, without being able to articulate why. The pastor who can name and explain the difference is equipped to help the congregation engage Scripture more thoughtfully, and to hold the differences with the mutual respect that brothers and sisters in Christ owe each other.

The differences cluster around three questions: (1) How should the Old Testament promises to Israel be interpreted? (2) Is the hermeneutical principle of "literalism" consistently applied? (3) What is the relationship between Israel and the Church? These are not peripheral questions — they shape the interpretation of large swathes of both Testaments. But they are questions on which godly, careful, Bible-loving scholars have reached different conclusions, and that fact alone should make both sides humble.
5.theology:
The Reformed (Covenant-Theological) approach: The Reformed tradition reads the Bible through the lens of the one Covenant of Grace, administered progressively through the biblical covenants (Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, New). The Church is the covenant people of God under the New Covenant — the continuation and expansion of Old Testament Israel, now including Gentiles on equal terms. Old Testament promises to Israel find their fulfillment typologically and spiritually in Christ and in his multiethnic body, the Church. The land promise to Abraham, for example, is fulfilled in the inheritance of the new creation (Rom 4:13; Heb 11:10, 16). The Davidic throne promise is fulfilled in Christ's heavenly reign (Acts 2:30–36). There is one people of God across both Testaments — the elect of all ages — and no essential distinction between Israel and the Church. The Millennium of Revelation 20 is typically understood as the present age of Christ's heavenly reign (amillennialism) or as a future golden age growing out of the gospel's spread (postmillennialism).

The Dispensational approach: The Dispensational tradition, developed by J.N. Darby and systematised by Scofield, Chafer, Ryrie, and Walvoord, insists that the Old Testament promises to Israel must be interpreted literally and that they retain their reference to the ethnic, national people of Israel. Israel and the Church are two distinct peoples with two distinct programmes in God's redemptive plan. The Church is a parenthesis in God's dealing with Israel — not anticipated in the Old Testament (Eph 3:3–6, the "mystery") — and will be removed at the Rapture so that God can resume and complete his programme for Israel in the Tribulation and Millennium. The Millennium is a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth, centred in Jerusalem, fulfilling the Davidic and Abrahamic promises to ethnic Israel. Progressive Dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock, Saucy) have modified the strict Israel-Church distinction while retaining a future for ethnic Israel and a literal millennium.

Key texts in dispute — and the principle of charitable engagement: Romans 9–11, Revelation 20, Galatians 3–4, Ephesians 2–3, and the land promises of Genesis 12–17 are the primary contested texts. Both traditions have developed sophisticated exegetical arguments for their positions. The pastoral wisdom is this: where both positions are represented in your congregation, teach the texts themselves with honesty about the interpretive options, model respectful disagreement, and keep the focus on the vast common ground — the authority of Scripture, the centrality of Christ, the necessity of faith, the certainty of resurrection, the hope of Christ's return. The hermeneutical differences are real; the fellowship in the gospel is deeper still.
5.examples:
Romans 11:26 — "All Israel will be saved": This text crystallises the debate. Reformed interpreters typically read "all Israel" as the full number of the elect from both Jews and Gentiles — the true Israel of God (Gal 6:16). Dispensational interpreters read it as ethnic Israel — the Jewish nation will, at the end of the age, turn to their Messiah in unprecedented numbers. The text itself does not resolve the debate with absolute clarity; serious scholars hold both positions. The preacher who acknowledges this — who says "here is what both traditions argue and why, here is where I land and why, and here is what we agree on regardless" — is modelling intellectual honesty and pastoral wisdom.

Amos 9:11–12 in Acts 15:16–18: James, at the Jerusalem Council, quotes Amos 9:11 (the restoration of David's fallen tent) and applies it to the inclusion of Gentiles in the church. Dispensationalists note that in context, Amos 9 speaks of the restoration of Israel's national fortunes — and argue that James is quoting the Septuagint to find a precedent for Gentile inclusion, not claiming that this is the fulfillment of Amos's primary prediction. Reformed interpreters argue that James is claiming precisely that — the restoration of David's tent is being fulfilled in the gathered, multiethnic church. This exegetical debate — contested at the highest scholarly levels — illustrates how the same text, read with the same grammatical-historical tools, can be read differently by people with different prior commitments about the Israel-Church relationship.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Reformed interpretation finds here a clear statement of the Church's continuity with Israel: Gentile believers, united to Christ by faith, are Abraham's offspring and heirs of the promise. The promise to Abraham — blessing for all nations (Gen 12:3) — is fulfilled in the worldwide, multiethnic community of those who are Christ's. Dispensational interpreters agree that Gentile believers are spiritual heirs of Abraham's blessing but distinguish this from the national-ethnic promises to Israel regarding land and kingdom, which they understand as remaining to be literally fulfilled for ethnic Israel. The text itself speaks of the Abrahamic promise; the debate is which dimensions of that promise are in view.

verseByVerse.quote: I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Both traditions take this text seriously and agree on its central claim: God has not and will not reject ethnic Israel. Dispensationalists find here confirmation that ethnic Israel has a distinct and continuing place in God's programme — Paul's own Jewishness is evidence that God's covenant faithfulness to Israel is not vacated by the Church age. Reformed interpreters agree that ethnic Jews are not excluded from salvation and that Romans 9–11 anticipates a significant future ingathering of Jewish people into the Church. The debate is whether "his people" refers to ethnic Israel as such or to the elect within Israel. Both traditions affirm God's faithfulness; they disagree about what that faithfulness entails.

verseByVerse.quote: This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is crucial for the Dispensational argument that the Church is a mystery unrevealed in the Old Testament. The Gentiles' inclusion as fellow heirs, members of the same body — on equal footing with Jewish believers — is what was hidden and is now revealed (v.3–5). Dispensationalists argue this demonstrates that the Church is a distinct new entity, not anticipated by Old Testament prophecy. Reformed interpreters note that Paul says the mystery was hidden, not that Gentile inclusion was unintended in the Old Testament — and that the mystery is the manner of inclusion (as fellow members of one body, without first becoming Jews) rather than the fact of Gentile blessing (always promised, Gen 12:3). The text repays careful study in both traditions.

verseByVerse.quote: Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's Pentecost sermon applies the Davidic throne promise to Jesus' resurrection and ascension: David foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of the Christ (v.31), and the risen Christ has been exalted to God's right hand (v.33). For Reformed interpreters, this is the fulfillment of the Davidic covenant — Christ reigns now from heaven, at the Father's right hand, and the Davidic promise is presently and fully operative. For Dispensational interpreters, this is a partial fulfillment — Christ is seated at the Father's right hand, but the throne of David (an earthly throne, in Jerusalem) is yet to be occupied at the Second Coming. The honest interpreter notes that Peter does not qualify his claim — but also that the Davidic covenant's original terms (2 Sam 7) specified an earthly dynasty. Both readings are serious engagements with a difficult text.

6.title: Preaching and Application: From Text to Congregation
6.overview:
The ultimate purpose of hermeneutics is not academic but doxological: that the congregation of God might hear the Word of God and be transformed by it. All the skills of the previous units — grammatical precision, historical contextualisation, biblical-theological placement, typological awareness, sensitivity to interpretive traditions — are in the service of this one end: the living Word landing on the living people of God with power, clarity, and love.

The move from text to sermon is called the homiletical bridge: taking what the text meant in its original context and expressing what it means for this congregation in this moment without losing the exegetical truth or imposing an alien application. This is harder than it sounds — the temptation on one side is to stay in the ancient world (a lecture on historical background, interesting but not preached), and on the other side to jump immediately to application without earning it from the text (relevant but not biblical).

The principle that governs the move is theological: the same God who acted then acts now. The same Word that addressed them addresses us. The same Spirit who inspired the text illumines us. The timeless theological truth of the passage — derived from careful exegesis — is the bridge from then to now. The specific application flows from that truth into the particular contours of the congregation's life.

Three questions drive faithful application: (1) What does this passage reveal about God — his character, his acts, his purposes? (2) What does it reveal about the human condition — our sin, our need, our dignity? (3) What is the good news — how does this passage point to or flow from the gospel of Christ? The sermon that answers all three questions, from the text, in the right order, is a biblical sermon. The congregation that hears it has encountered the living God through his written Word.
6.theology:
The "Big Idea" method: Haddon Robinson's influential approach to expository preaching centers on identifying the "Big Idea" of the passage — the single central claim that drives the text — and allowing every element of the sermon to serve that idea. This is a hermeneutical discipline before it is a homiletical one: you cannot preach one clear idea from a text until you have understood what the text is saying. The discipline of distilling the text to its central claim is excellent exegetical training.

Redemptive-historical preaching: Bryan Chapell's "Christ-centred preaching" and the broader redemptive-historical tradition (Clowney, Goldsworthy, Greidanus) insist that every passage of Scripture — Old Testament as well as New — should be preached in light of Christ's work. This does not mean forcing a gospel ending onto every sermon regardless of the text's context; it means recognising that every text exists within the story of redemption and gains its fullest meaning in light of its place in that story. Old Testament narrative, preached redemptive-historically, becomes far richer than moral example — it becomes part of the story of the God who saves.

Law and gospel in application: The Reformed tradition's careful distinction between law (what God demands) and gospel (what God gives in Christ) is crucial for application. Every text has some relationship to this distinction — it either convicts (law) or comforts and transforms (gospel), or both in sequence. The preacher who does not know which is doing which will produce either guilt without grace (law without gospel) or cheap grace without repentance (gospel without law). The congregation needs both, in the right proportion, from every text.
6.examples:
Spurgeon on connecting old texts to Christ: Charles Spurgeon preached from every corner of the Bible and always found his way to Christ. "I take my text and make a beeline to the cross" — this was not a failure of exegetical discipline but the expression of a deep conviction that every text exists within the story of the cross and that the congregation needs to see Christ in every Scripture. The preacher who can make that beeline faithfully — without bypassing the exegesis — has mastered the hermeneutical art.

Applying difficult commands: When Jesus says "cut off your hand if it causes you to sin" (Matt 5:30), the grammatical-historical method immediately notes the hyperbole — a common rhetorical device in Near Eastern teaching, used to startle the listener into attention. The literal application (physical self-mutilation) would be both physically harmful and theologically incorrect — Jesus is addressing the heart, not the hand. The application is radical discipleship in dealing with temptation, not surgery. Genre recognition and literary sensitivity are essential tools for faithful application.

verseByVerse.quote: For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's warrant for applying the Old Testament to New Testament believers: everything written in the former days was written for our instruction. Not merely their instruction. Ours. This is both a hermeneutical permission (we may apply Old Testament texts to ourselves) and a hermeneutical obligation (we must not leave the Old Testament in the ancient world as though it has nothing to say to us). The goal of that application is practical and pastoral: endurance and encouragement leading to hope. The preacher who brings an Old Testament text to the congregation with this in mind will not merely inform them — they will strengthen them for the journey.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Exodus narratives are not merely ancient history — they are examples for us (Greek: tupoi — types). The application Paul draws is both negative (do not desire evil as they did) and positive (be warned, and turn from temptation). This is responsible typological application: Paul identifies the pattern (Israel's wilderness failure), notes the type, and draws the application for the New Testament congregation. He does not say "this is exactly our situation"; he says "this is a pattern that speaks to our situation." That is the homiletical move: from then to now, through the theological truth that the same God is at work with the same kinds of people in the same kind of world.

verseByVerse.quote: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: All hermeneutics is finally in the service of this: not merely understanding the Word but doing it. The sophistication of one's interpretive method is a means, not an end. The end is a transformed life — a congregation that hears the Word clearly, receives it humbly, and obeys it consistently. James's warning is severe: the person who hears without doing is a self-deceiver. They have received the information without the formation. The preacher's task is not complete when the exegesis is accurate and the application is clear — it is complete when the Spirit has used both to move the hearer toward doing. That final step belongs to the Spirit. The preacher can only be faithful to the text and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The great comfort of the preacher and the great comfort of hermeneutics. The Word of God does not return empty. The sermon that is faithful to the text — however imperfectly delivered, however small the congregation, however resistant the hearers — is a word sent by God, and it will accomplish what God purposes. The interpreter's responsibility is faithfulness to the text; the Word's effectiveness is God's responsibility. This frees the preacher from the tyranny of results and grounds them in the freedom of obedience: preach the Word, in season and out of season (2 Tim 4:2), and trust that the One who sent it will ensure it lands where he intends.
